source: Flavell (1979) Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: a new area of cognitive-developmental inquiry
finding: Coined metacognition. Splits it into metacognitive knowledge (person, task, strategy variables), metacognitive experiences, goals, and actions. Monitoring happens through the interplay of these four.
numbers: Not read this session; no figures recorded. Theory paper.
limits: Taken from secondary summaries and the SUBFIELDS file, not the paper text. Conceptual, no experiment.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary: strategy knowledge ('when does operator X work') is what a class record could hold; a 'metacognitive experience' (feeling of difficulty) must become a coded signal.

source: Brown (1978, 1987) Knowing, learning and understanding; Metacognition, executive control, self-regulation
finding: Brown framed the regulation side as executive control: planning, monitoring, checking and revising. She noted that learners who lack these skills fail even with adequate knowledge.
numbers: Not read this session; no figures recorded.
limits: Secondary summary only. Brown's work on children's reading and memory strategy training is the empirical base; effects were task-specific.
agent_relevance: Source of the plan/monitor/evaluate triple. Maps to S-states: plan before acting, monitor during, evaluate after, each as a code-checked step.

source: Nelson and Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Two levels: object level and meta level. Monitoring sends information up. Control sends commands down (continue, stop, switch strategy, allocate time). This is the standard formal frame for regulation.
numbers: Not read this session; no figures recorded.
limits: Secondary only. Built on memory tasks (judgments of learning, feeling of knowing), where monitoring accuracy is the bottleneck.
agent_relevance: Direct template for the schema: object level = model attempt, meta level = program. Control quality depends on monitoring quality, so monitor with code checks, not model self-report.

source: Swanson (1990) Influence of metacognitive knowledge and aptitude on problem solving. J Educational Psychology 82, 306-314
finding: Children were crossed on aptitude (high/low) and metacognition (high/low). High-metacognition children beat low-metacognition children on problem solving whatever their aptitude. Metacognition seemed to compensate for low aptitude.
numbers: 2 x 2 design on a pendulum task and a second task. Exact N, means and effect sizes not verified (abstract and citing papers only).
quote: high levels of metacognitive knowledge ... compensate for low overall aptitude
limits: A later critique says forcing intelligence and metacognition to be orthogonal factors by design limits what the study can show. Metacognition was measured by interview of knowledge, not by observed regulation. Children, two tasks.
agent_relevance: The subfield's headline claim. Weak support for an agent: compensation was shown in humans by taught knowledge, and a model has no such aptitude/metacognition split. Treat as motivation, not proof.

source: Perkins and Salomon (1989) Are cognitive skills context-bound? Educational Researcher 18(1), 16-25
finding: General strategies (including metacognitive ones) can be useful, but they transfer only when taught with real content and with cues to apply them. The 'high road' of transfer needs mindful abstraction; the 'low road' is practised routine.
numbers: Review; no pooled figures.
limits: Only secondary summaries read. The review predates later meta-analyses, which find larger effects when training is embedded in subject content.
agent_relevance: Supports putting the regulation prompt inside the task context (S6 trigger tied to a concrete failing output) rather than a generic 'check your work' line.

source: Schraw and Dennison (1994) Assessing metacognitive awareness. Contemporary Educational Psychology 19, 460-475
finding: Built the 52-item Metacognitive Awareness Inventory. Two factors: knowledge of cognition and regulation of cognition. Regulation has five subprocesses: planning, information management, monitoring, debugging, evaluation.
numbers: Two experiments, 307 undergraduates in total (179 in Experiment 1). Reliability alpha = .90 (reported by citing papers). Factors intercorrelated around r = .50 per a citing paper.
limits: Self-report. A later study found only 25 of 52 items loaded cleanly on two factors. Not read in full; one ERIC paper that cites it was opened but it gave no detail.
agent_relevance: Gives a five-part taxonomy of regulation to test against our states: planning (S-plan), monitoring (progress detector), debugging (repair operator), evaluation (review).

source: Veenman, Van Hout-Wolters and Afflerbach (2006) Metacognition and learning: conceptual and methodological considerations. Metacognition and Learning 1, 3-14
finding: Metacognitive skillfulness is only partly the same as intellectual ability and adds to learning performance on its own. The paper argues for on-line measures (think-aloud, observation) over questionnaires.
numbers: Percent-of-variance figures I had in mind (about 10 to 17 percent unique) could not be verified this session; not recorded as fact.
limits: Search returned only bibliographic details and a secondary summary. The paper is an editorial review, not a single study.
agent_relevance: Supports measuring the agent's regulation by observed behaviour (logged switches, checks) not by what it says about itself.

source: Mevarech and Kramarski (1997) IMPROVE: a multidimensional method for teaching mathematics in heterogeneous classrooms. AERJ 34, 365-394
finding: Students used cards with metacognitive self-questions (comprehension, connection, strategy, reflection) plus cooperative learning and feedback. IMPROVE students beat controls on several math measures, most in reasoning.
numbers: One study followed N = 265 over a school year. Exact effect sizes not verified.
limits: Three components applied together, so metacognitive questions cannot be isolated. A 2008 follow-up reported gains in regulation of cognition but not in knowledge about cognition. Transfer untested.
agent_relevance: Closest human match to 'Is it getting me anywhere?' self-questions. Note: the human gain came with feedback and peers, which the agent does not have unless code supplies the check.

source: Dent and Koenka (2015/2016) The relation between self-regulated learning and academic achievement across childhood and adolescence: a meta-analysis (as summarised by globalmetacognition.com)
finding: Metacognitive processes correlate with achievement more than plain cognitive strategies do. On-line measures were more accurate than off-line. Planning was significant. Rote memorisation was weaker or negative.
numbers: Metacognitive processes r = 0.20; cognitive strategies r = 0.11. Study count not stated on the page.
limits: Opened a secondary summary page, not the paper. Correlational. Page says it is a synthesis of two meta-analyses.
agent_relevance: Shows the effect is modest in humans (r about .2). Do not expect a large lift from a metacognitive layer alone.

source: Ohtani and Hisasaka (2018) Beyond intelligence: a meta-analytic review of metacognition, intelligence and academic performance (via globalmetacognition.com)
finding: Metacognition predicts performance beyond intelligence, and the link is far stronger with on-line measures than with questionnaires. This partly supports Swanson's independence claim.
numbers: On-line measures r = .53; off-line r = .23. In on-line studies, beta = .41 for metacognition vs beta = .32 for intelligence. A search summary gave 149 samples from 118 articles (not opened).
limits: Secondary page. Springer paper blocked behind login. Correlational, so metacognition may be a marker of effort.
agent_relevance: The measurement lesson again: observed regulation behaviour predicts outcomes; self-report does not. Log actions.

source: Muncer et al. (2021) metacognition and mathematics performance meta-analysis (via globalmetacognition.com)
finding: Metacognition relates to math performance, more so on-line and on complex tasks.
numbers: 31 studies, over 570,000 students. Overall r = .37; on-line r > .40; complex maths tasks r = .54.
limits: Secondary page. Correlational. | CORRECTION (cross-check, Muncer PDF opened): complex-task alone r = .48 (n=12,k=21); online r = .54 (n=9,k=14) vs offline .30; online x complex cell r = .54 (n=13, omnibus p=.058, marginal). 'Complex r=.54' is wrong.
agent_relevance: Regulation matters more on complex tasks. Suggests gating regulation by difficulty, not applying it to easy items (see overthinking, a24).

source: De Boer et al. (2018); Theobald (2021); Higgins et al. (2005); Dignath and Buttner (2008) intervention meta-analyses (via globalmetacognition.com)
finding: Teaching metacognitive and self-regulation strategies raises achievement in humans, medium to large in short term.
numbers: De Boer: 48 interventions, g = 0.50 immediate, 0.63 follow-up. Theobald: 49 studies, g = 0.37 overall, metacognitive strategies g = 0.40. Higgins: 29 studies, metacognitive interventions 0.96. Dignath and Buttner: 74 studies, 357 effect sizes, mean 0.69; researchers beat regular teachers. Eberhart: immediate g = 0.48, longer-term g = 0.29.
limits: Secondary page. Effects shrink at follow-up and when teachers deliver instead of researchers. Mostly school children and students; effect sizes are inflated by researcher-designed tests.
agent_relevance: Human training gains are real but fade and depend on the implementer. Our agent has no training, so only the structure carries over.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive capabilities of LLMs: an exploration in mathematical problem solving. arXiv 2405.12205
finding: GPT-4 names the skill each math question needs and clusters skills. At test time the LLM picks the needed skill label, then gets exemplars tagged with it. This beats plain chain of thought on MATH and GSM8K.
numbers: MATH: +11.6% over CoT, +3.5% over Complex CoT and over topic-based exemplars. Code (PAL): +7.52%. With self-consistency: +4.0% over CoT-SC. Skills from GPT-4 also helped Mixtral 8x7B.
limits: Needs a strong model to build the skill repository. Gains are in-context retrieval of examples, a form of strategy knowledge, not monitoring. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Evidence that metacognitive knowledge (which skill applies) is codable and learnable into a class record, matching open question 2 in SUBFIELDS.

source: Wang and Zhao (2024) Metacognitive prompting improves understanding in large language models. arXiv 2308.05342
finding: A five-stage prompt (understand, judge, evaluate, decide, assess confidence) gives modest gains on ten NLU datasets over CoT and plan-and-solve.
numbers: Zero-shot MP gains 4.8% to 6.4% over CoT and 2.8% to 4.1% over PS (averaged per model). Five-shot M-MP gains 4.5% to 6.0% over M-CoT and 2.2% to 3.5% over CoT-SC. GPT-4 zero-shot MP: 89.9/86.2 on QQP vs 88.9/84.7 for CoT; UNFAIR-ToS 64.0/45.3 vs 54.7/38.5.
limits: Four models, ten NLU classification sets. Authors report overthinking errors under MP. The introspective stages are the model judging itself with no external check.
agent_relevance: Prompt-only regulation gives small gains on understanding tasks. Does not show gains on reasoning with checkable answers. Matches G1: do not apply on a schedule.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet. ICLR. arXiv 2310.01798
finding: Without an oracle label, asking a model to review and revise its answer lowers accuracy. Earlier gains came from using ground truth to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 (round 1) -> 41.8 (round 2). GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. GPT-4 CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 -> 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 97.5, CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 -> 59.0 (columns reconstructed from garbled PDF text). GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K; changes were more often right-to-wrong.
limits: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2 and 2023 prompts. Later work shows trained models can improve (a20). Evaluation subsets of 100 to 1,000 items.
agent_relevance: Core support for G2 and G1: the model cannot judge its own reasoning. Evaluation must come from code or held-out checks, never from the model's opinion.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction. arXiv 2406.01297
finding: No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs in general tasks. It works where reliable external feedback exists, with large-scale fine-tuning, or on tasks exceptionally suited (decomposable responses). The bottleneck is feedback generation.
numbers: Survey; no pooled number. Three conclusions: no demonstrated prompted-LLM self-correction in general tasks; works with reliable external feedback; large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
limits: Survey of papers to mid-2024. Provides a checklist: many papers use unfair comparisons or oracle stopping.
agent_relevance: Strongest summary for S6: put the review step on code-produced feedback (tests, held-out, mutated input), not model-produced critique.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location. arXiv 2311.08516
finding: Splits regulation into mistake finding (monitoring) and correction (control). Models are poor at the first and good at the second.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake has 2,186 step-annotated CoT traces. GPT-4 reaches only 52.87 overall accuracy on mistake finding with direct step-level prompting (tasks from 17.06 to 90.67 by condition). With the true mistake location, backtracking gains outweigh losses; a random location gives much smaller gains. A small classifier trained on out-of-domain data finds mistakes better than prompting a large model.
limits: Five models (GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, Gemini Pro, PaLM 2 Unicorn) and five reasoning tasks; traces from PaLM 2. Mistake location comes from human labels in the correction test.
agent_relevance: Maps cleanly onto the Nelson-Narens frame: monitoring is the weak part, control is fine. Spend effort on code that locates the failure, then let the model fix it (G2).

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback. arXiv 2303.17651
finding: Generate, critique own output, refine, repeat. Big gains on open-ended style tasks, almost none on math where the model cannot spot errors.
numbers: Claimed 20% absolute average gain over seven tasks. Dialogue (GPT-3.5) 36.4 -> 63.6; code readability 37.4 -> 51.3; code optimisation 14.8 -> 23.0. Math reasoning (GPT-3.5) 64.1 -> 64.1 (0 gain). ChatGPT feedback on math said 'everything looks good' for 94% of instances; with an external signal of correctness, math gains exceed 5%.
limits: Gains are on preference-judged tasks with model and GPT-4 judges. Math shows the limit. Not a failure to replicate but later work (a15) shows reasoning gains vanish without external signal.
agent_relevance: Regulation by self-feedback helps where quality is a matter of taste and fails where correctness is crisp; our tasks are the second kind, so use code checks.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning. arXiv 2303.11366
finding: After a failed trial, the agent writes a verbal reflection stored in memory and tries again. Triggers are code heuristics: same action and same response for more than 3 cycles, or more than 30 actions.
numbers: ALFWorld: 130 of 134 tasks solved with ReAct plus Reflexion over 12 trials; claims +22% over baseline. HotPotQA +20%. HumanEval pass@1 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1; MBPP 68.0 vs 60.0; LeetcodeHard 77.1 vs 80.1 (Reflexion below GPT-4 there). Memory kept to the last 3 reflections (1 for code).
limits: Relies on an environment or unit-test signal that says the trial failed. Test suite quality limits the code results. Gains depend on that external success signal (see a15, a16).
agent_relevance: Best-matching design for S6: a coded impasse trigger starts the reflection, and the failing output is cited. Confirms G1 and G2.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training language models to self-correct via reinforcement learning (SCoRe). arXiv 2409.12917
finding: Supervised fine-tuning on correction traces fails (distribution mismatch, behaviour collapse). Multi-turn RL on the model's own traces yields real intrinsic self-correction.
numbers: Gemini 1.0 Pro and 1.5 Flash. Self-correction gain +15.6% on MATH and +9.1% on HumanEval over base. On MATH Gemini 1.5 Flash, delta (t1 to t2) of +4.4% is the first clearly positive delta; Accuracy@t2 +23.0% over base; +10.2% and +2.6% over Pair-SFT. Fixes wrong answers at 14.5% vs 9.5% for base.
limits: Requires training, which our scaffold excludes. Gemini models only. Shows the capacity can be taught, so its absence in prompted models is not fundamental.
agent_relevance: Says the human-style gain from trained metacognition is real for LLMs too, but only via training. For a scaffold-only agent it points back to external checks.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know. arXiv 2207.05221
finding: Large models are calibrated on multiple-choice tasks. They can estimate P(True) for their own sample and be trained to predict P(IK), 'do I know this'. AUROC for P(IK) rises with model size.
numbers: Up to 52B-parameter models. 20-shot P(True) over five sampling tasks; restricting to answers with P(True) > 0.5 raises accuracy on each task. P(IK) generalises partly across tasks but calibration is weak on new tasks. Specific per-task values not extracted.
limits: 2022 base models; RLHF calibration needs temperature fix. Calibration on a held-in distribution, weaker out of distribution. Contrasts with a15 where reasoning self-judgment fails.
agent_relevance: A weak, usable monitoring signal exists (P(True) on sampled answers), but SCHEMA says stated confidence is not a monitor. Could be a cheap tie-breaker, never a gate (G5).

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: large language models self-compose reasoning structures. arXiv 2402.03620
finding: Planning step: the model selects, adapts and implements atomic reasoning modules into a task-level structure once, then follows it per instance. Planning before solving is cheap.
numbers: Up to +32% over CoT (BigBench-Hard, T4D, MATH). Average BBH +11% (PaLM 2-L) and +7% (GPT-4); T4D +39% and +29%. Beats CoT self-consistency by more than 20% with 10 to 40 times less inference compute.
limits: Task-level plan from unlabelled examples; tested on PaLM 2-L, GPT-4, Llama2. Gains concentrated in tasks where a structure helps.
agent_relevance: Planning (the first regulation component) is the best-supported piece for LLMs and is cheap. Fits an S-plan state done once per class.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve prompting. arXiv 2305.04091
finding: Devise a plan first, then carry it out. Targets missing-step errors of zero-shot CoT. PS+ adds extraction of variables and care in calculation.
numbers: text-davinci-003 zero-shot averages over six math sets: CoT 70.4, PS 73.5, PS+ 76.7 (vs 77.6 for few-shot Manual-CoT). GSM8K: CoT 56.4, PS 57.0, PS+ 59.3. Error analysis of 46 GSM8K problems: calculation 7%, missing-step 12%, semantic misunderstanding 27%.
limits: Old model, a single sampling setting. Gain on GSM8K is small (about 3 points).
agent_relevance: Plan-first is a small but cheap win; it shows planning alone does not fix the monitoring problem.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs. arXiv 2412.21187
finding: Reasoning models fail the 'is it getting me anywhere' check on easy questions. They add solutions that do not improve accuracy. First-correct solution usually appears early.
numbers: On '2 plus 3' o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. 13 solutions for one trivial question. Self-training cut tokens by 48.6% on MATH500 for QwQ-32B-Preview with accuracy kept. Overthinking is more frequent on easy problems.
limits: QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1 class models; math sets (GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME). Fix requires training on shortened responses.
agent_relevance: Regulation must include a stop rule: when the check passes, stop (G1). Progress monitoring is a stopping problem, linked to the optimal-stopping and meta-reasoning subfields.

source: Nezhurina et al. (2025) Alice in Wonderland: simple tasks showing complete reasoning breakdown in state-of-the-art LLMs. arXiv 2406.02061
finding: Downloaded and not read beyond the title page. Reported to show that strong models fail on a simple reasoning task while stating high confidence, i.e. poor self-monitoring.
numbers: No figures taken; not read.
limits: Not read this session. Do not cite for numbers until opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate for the monitoring-failure line of evidence; open in the next pass.

source: Kamoi et al. and Huang et al. read together: oracle stop signal versus intrinsic stop signal (synthesis of a15, a16, a19)
finding: Reflexion, Self-Refine and RCI report gains that rely on a ground-truth or tool signal that says when to stop. Remove it and gains turn into losses. The difference between the two settings is the monitoring signal, not the reflection prompt.
numbers: GPT-4 HotpotQA 49 -> 59 with oracle labels (Huang et al. Table 2); GSM8K GPT-4 95.5 -> 89.0 intrinsic after 2 rounds.
limits: A synthesis of read sources, not an independent study.
agent_relevance: Design rule: the S6 trigger and the evaluation are both code. The model writes a repair only once the trigger fires and a real failing output is shown.
